content: Tonsillitis is an infection and inflammation of the tonsils, which are lymphoid tissues located at the back of the throat. It typically manifests as a sore throat accompanied by fever. The tonsils are covered by a protective membrane, and in cases where removal is necessary, a surgical procedure called tonsillectomy is performed. Tonsillitis can be classified into several types: Acute tonsillitis: This can be caused by bacterial or viral pathogens. Subacute tonsillitis: This is most commonly caused by the bacterium Actinomyces. Chronic tonsillitis: This is associated with conditions such as allergies, asthma, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), viral infections like Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), or bacterial infections. Recurrent tonsillitis: This involves repeated episodes of tonsillitis. The pathophysiology of tonsillitis involves the infection of the tonsils by either viral or bacterial pathogens, which triggers an inflammatory response. Viral tonsillitis occurs when viruses infiltrate the tonsils, leading to an upregulation of cytokines and subsequent inflammation. Acute bacterial tonsillitis is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A β-hemolytic streptococcus, GABHS). These bacteria penetrate the tonsillar epithelium by breaching the protective mucosal barriers of the oral and nasal cavities. Recurrent bacterial tonsillitis is often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, which invades non-phagocytic cells via fibronectin-binding proteins and beta-integrins, leading to cytokine upregulation and inflammation. Tonsillitis is associated with various viral and bacterial pathogens. The most common viral causes include adenovirus, rhinovirus, influenza virus, coronavirus, and respiratory syncytial virus. Other potential viral causes include Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV. In rare cases, tonsillitis may result from a superinfection with spirochetes and Treponema, known as Vincent’s angina or Plaut-Vincent angina. Differentiating tonsillitis from other diseases is essential, as other conditions may present with similar symptoms, such as tonsillar and nasopharyngeal edema, erythema, lymphadenopathy, fever, dysphonia, and dysphagia. The epidemiology of tonsillitis is not fully understood. Research suggests that bacterial tonsillitis accounts for 15-30% of sore throats in children and 5-10% in adults. Studies indicate a prevalence of approximately 11,700 cases per 100,000 individuals in Norwegian twins and 12,100 cases per 100,000 primary school children in Turkey. Acute tonsillitis caused by S. pyogenes primarily affects children aged 5 to 15 years. Tonsillitis is more common in females than males, with no racial or demographic predisposition. The case fatality rate is unknown. Risk factors for tonsillitis include environmental and systemic factors that increase susceptibility to pathogenic viral or bacterial invasion. Acute tonsillitis typically presents with rapid onset of tonsillar erythema and edema following pathogen infiltration. It is usually self-limiting, with symptoms resolving within 3-4 days. Recurrent tonsillitis, however, often requires antimicrobial therapy or tonsillectomy. Complications arise from the persistence or spread of the responsible pathogen, usually bacterial. The prognosis for untreated acute tonsillitis is generally good, while untreated recurrent tonsillitis may lead to life-threatening complications. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis for both acute and recurrent tonsillitis is favorable. The diagnosis of tonsillitis is primarily clinical. Symptoms include severe sore throat (which may radiate to the ears), painful or difficult swallowing, headache, fever, chills, and a characteristic hot potato voice. Other symptoms may include localized pain in the head, neck, and throat, coughing, systemic symptoms like fever and swollen cervical lymph nodes, and less commonly, nausea, vomiting, furry tongue, halitosis, and difficulty opening the mouth. Physical examination findings include tonsillar erythema, edema, and exudate, along with cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and dysphonia. Patients often appear ill, with malaise and lethargy due to fever. Laboratory confirmation of GABHS tonsillitis can be achieved through throat swabs and culture, with samples plated on sheep blood agar. Anaerobic incubation and selective media can improve isolation rates. Treatment of tonsillitis involves antimicrobial therapy and analgesics. Supportive measures include saltwater gargles and lozenges. Penicillin is the first-line antibiotic, with alternatives such as cephalosporins, clindamycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, or amoxicillin for those allergic to penicillin. Pain management may involve topical anesthetics like viscous lidocaine solutions and systemic analgesics like ibuprofen to reduce inflammation and facilitate swallowing. Viral tonsillitis typically resolves within one week, though some infections may last up to two weeks. Warm saltwater gargles can help alleviate pain and swelling. Chronic or recurrent cases may necessitate tonsillectomy, the surgical removal of the tonsils. Prevention of tonsillitis includes proper hygienic practices and avoiding contact with individuals with contagious infections. Primary prevention measures include: Proper handwashing and hand antisepsis. Selection of appropriate hand hygiene antimicrobial agents. Facial cleanliness. Proper dental hygiene. Avoiding contact between hands, eyes, mouth, and infectious agents. Secondary prevention involves the use of antibiotics to prevent recurrent tonsillitis.
